The transverse flute reached Europe from Asia, probably by way of Byzantium, and appears in the writings of Adenet le Roi in 1285; in the 1470s it spread through its use for Swiss army signals, and at the end of the sixteenth century it entered the court, the theatre and chamber music. In the Baroque period it was redesigned as the traverso (Baroque flute), with a conical bore, three or four joints and one key, giving a wider and more penetrating range. In the nineteenth century Theobald Boehm patented a key system in 1847, moving to metal, large toneholes and linked keys, and this established the modern flute.
